# What you said, and what you picked

*Divergence report for Eric Vossberg, an invented persona. Generated by `npm run calibrate`.*

**How this was made.** You compared 600 pairs of people, one choice at a time. A small, readable model (a logistic regression on differences between the two people) was fitted to those choices and nothing else. Below, every claim is either something you said or something your choices show, with the evidence next to it. You can disagree with any line.

> **Read this first.** Eric is fictional and so are his labels. They come from a latent preference function we wrote on purpose to contradict his stated profile. The question this report answers is whether the method can find that gap from the labels alone and state it plainly. It is a validation on synthetic ground truth, not a discovery about a person. See the eval report for the grading against the truth.

## The short version

You asked for someone mobile and unanchored. In the 200 comparisons where one person fitted that description clearly better than the other, you picked the better fit 8% of the time (16 of 200; 95% interval 5% to 13%). Chance is 50%.

Your choices contradict your stated profile on **4** points: work needs a place, old local friendships, years in city, nights away per month.

## Where you said one thing and chose another

### work needs a place

- **You said:** "independent ... not waiting on me": portable work fits a mobile partner (implied). That implies a person who does work that can be done from anywhere.
- **Your choices say:** you pick the person who does work that cannot be done from an airport lounge.
- **Evidence from the raw choices:** when the two people clearly differed, you picked the one who does work that cannot be done from an airport lounge 86% of the time (271 of 314; 95% interval 82% to 90%).
- **Model weight:** +0.45 logits per standard deviation (90% interval +0.25 to +0.68).

### old local friendships

- **You said:** "unanchored" (implied). That implies a person who has few long-standing local friendships.
- **Your choices say:** you pick the person who has long-standing local friendships.
- **Evidence from the raw choices:** when the two people clearly differed, you picked the one who has long-standing local friendships 80% of the time (296 of 372; 95% interval 75% to 83%).
- **Model weight:** +0.40 logits per standard deviation (90% interval +0.21 to +0.62).

### years in city

- **You said:** "as mobile and unanchored as he is" (explicit). That implies a person who has only recently arrived in their city.
- **Your choices say:** you pick the person who has lived in their city for years.
- **Evidence from the raw choices:** when the two people clearly differed, you picked the one who has lived in their city for years 79% of the time (340 of 431; 95% interval 75% to 82%).
- **Model weight:** +0.33 logits per standard deviation (90% interval +0.15 to +0.56).

### nights away per month

- **You said:** "I travel constantly. I need someone who gets that"; "someone I can see in two cities" (explicit). That implies a person who is away from home many nights a month.
- **Your choices say:** you pick the person who is rarely away from home.
- **Evidence from the raw choices:** when the two people clearly differed, you picked the one who is away from home many nights a month 23% of the time (74 of 325; 95% interval 19% to 28%).
- **Model weight:** -0.30 logits per standard deviation (90% interval -0.51 to -0.11).

### Three of your own choices, side by side

- You picked **Gezetio Emberbury** (climbing gym coach, 12 years in Utrecht, 0 nights away a month, has a practice tied to a place) over **Daniozae Nettlefield** (airline crew, 1 year in Barcelona, 16 nights away a month), although the second fits "mobile and unanchored" better.
- You picked **Tiotuhel Emberfield** (secondary school teacher, 14 years in Paris, 1 night away a month) over **Tiliasis Embercombe** (airline crew, 0 years in Milan, 28 nights away a month), although the second fits "mobile and unanchored" better.
- You picked **Sisinun Juniperthorn** (restaurant chef, 11 years in Madrid, 1 night away a month, has a practice tied to a place) over **Sioriahom Ironcombe** (airline crew, 2 years in Utrecht, 14 nights away a month), although the second fits "mobile and unanchored" better.

## What you did not say but your choices show

- **physical practice**: you pick the person who runs or belongs to a practice with a physical place (weight +0.27, 90% interval +0.08 to +0.47; picked the higher one 80% of 300 clear comparisons).
- (weak lead) **photo urban**: you pick the person who is photographed in a city setting (weight +0.17, 90% interval +0.02 to +0.33; picked the higher one 69% of 127 clear comparisons).
With 23 features, one or two weak effects at the edge of their interval are expected by chance alone. A "weak lead" is an effect whose interval comes within 0.05 of zero: treat it as a question to ask, not a finding.

## Where your words hold up, or the labels are silent

- **job tenure years**: you said this; the labels show no clear effect (+0.10, 90% interval -0.07 to +0.32).

## What this does and does not claim

- The weights describe your choices in this sitting. They are not a statement about why you choose, and they are not a rule: the funnel uses them to rank, never to reject. Rejection stays on the fields you declared.
- The visual features describe the photograph (setting, activity, solo or group, photo type, lighting, focus). There is no attractiveness measure anywhere, by design.
- Some choices will be noise (a tired thumb, a near-tie), and the model cannot tell which. It also cannot see anything particular to one person that does not show up in a feature.
- Scorer in the funnel: `learned-pairwise-v1`. Select it with `--scorer learned` in `npm run demo:learned`.
